Formulation:
Predisposing: History of intermittent anxiety.  
Precipitating: Acute physical trigger (insect sting) causing fear of severe allergic reaction.  
Perpetuating: Living alone, limited immediate reassurance, lack of prior experience managing similar events.  
Protective: Adequate health literacy, access to tele-health, employment stability, willingness to follow medical advice.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Situational anxiety / panic-type response to medical event
- Patient Goal(s): Understand bodily sensations after a sting; reduce anxiety; know when to seek urgent care.
- Clinical Goal(s): Provide education on normal versus dangerous reactions; teach basic anxiety-management strategies; monitor frequency/intensity of panic symptoms.
- Actions (Patient):
  • Read provided information on anaphylaxis and typical sting reactions.  
  • Take over-the-counter antihistamine as advised.  
  • Monitor breathing, lip/tongue swelling; seek emergency help if warning signs occur.  
  • Note anxiety episodes; consider keeping brief symptom diary.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Supply written information links (completed).  
  • Reassure and normalise mild local reaction.  
  • Offer follow-up appointment if anxiety persists or escalates.  
  • Consider referral for psychological support (e.g., brief CBT for anxiety) if episodes become recurrent.

Secondary Problem: Occasional baseline anxiety
- Patient Goal(s): Prevent future panic episodes; improve overall anxiety management.
- Clinical Goal(s): Screen for formal anxiety disorder at review; explore coping skills and support systems.
- Actions (Patient): Reflect on stressors; adopt relaxation techniques (to be provided at review).
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Schedule review; complete validated anxiety screening tool (e.g., GAD-7); discuss potential referral to counselling if indicated.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: Signs of anaphylaxis vs. local reaction; use of antihistamines; when to attend ED; reassurance regarding expected rash.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Swelling of lips/tongue, stridor, progressive breathlessness, escalating anxiety without medical cause.
- Coping Strategies: Information review; prompt medical contact for reassurance; (additional strategies to be discussed at follow-up).
